source.title: LIAR: Leveraging Inference Time Alignment (Best-of-N) to Jailbreak LLMs in Seconds
source.authors: James Beetham; Souradip Chakraborty; Mengdi Wang; Furong Huang; A. S. Bedi; Mubarak Shah

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether suffix-based attacks can bypass safety behaviour using a best-of-N inference-time attack and harmful-completion success rates; it does not reproduce the claim’s fine-tuning or token-position measurements.
record.gate_note: The study tests suffix attacks and reports attack success rates. It does not test fine-tuning, compliant-token prefilling, per-token KL concentration, safety localization in weights, or deepening safety training. Table 1's comparisons with GCG, AutoDAN, and AdvPrompter are not separately extracted here. Values cited from other studies are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: LIAR is a black-box best-of-N suffix attack on safety-trained chat models. It reports how often it bypasses refusal. That bears on V4's suffix clause only. The study does not test prefilling, fine-tuning, per-token KL, parameter localization, or deepening.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors present LIAR as a fast, training-free best-of-N suffix attack with low-perplexity prompts. They say it is hard to defend against and that it is unclear whether alignment can fully avoid harmful responses. They do not claim anything about fine-tuning or token-position depth.
record.recipe_differences: Uses an inference-time best-of-N suffix attack, not fine-tuning aligned models, compliant-token prefilling, or measuring aligned-versus-base token KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies with target model, adversarial suffix model, suffix-generation temperature, suffix length, target response length, dataset, and system-prompt condition. The text says ASR@100 peaks around temperature 0.6; ASR@10 peaks at suffix length 48 and ASR@100 at length 30. No-suffix results also vary with target decoding and system prompt.
record.problems: The authors state that the safety-net scores have run-to-run variance but do not report uncertainty estimates. ASR uses a keyword-matching aspect that can count prompt drift as success; examples include false positives. Most reported ASR results use only the first 30 target-response tokens, and the authors describe this as a compute-saving deviation from the more standard 150 tokens. Results vary sharply by target model.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix E.1 Tables 7-8 report additional adversarial-model/target combinations and are not extracted to keep the record focused on the main conditions and the separately varied settings. Appendix E.2 Table 9 reports more datasets and targets and is omitted. Table 1's GCG, AutoDAN, and AdvPrompter comparator results, as well as PAIR and BoN Jailbreak comparisons, are omitted because they are comparisons with other attack methods rather than separate LIAR conditions.

untested.parts: Per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Compliant-start prefilling and attacks that change target decoding. Sampling appears only in the no-suffix controls.
Causes of shallowness in data or objective.

missing.what: Results for Llama2, Llama3 and Llama3.1 targets across adversarial LLMs, showing ASR@100 mostly under 30 except Vicuna-7b
Results for Vicuna-7b and 13b on additional datasets: JailbreakBench, DoNotAnswer and the AdvBench train split
Results for other adversarial LLMs, such as Llama2-7b-chat used as the suffix generator

record.verdict_notes: The study bears only on the suffix part of V4. The ASR metric uses keyword matching over the first 30 response tokens. The authors say this can count prompt drift as success and give false positives (Table 11). ASR@100 is not comparable to single-attempt attacks. No uncertainty is reported. The record's label rows lump no-suffix controls and attack rows together, which blurs the evidence.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.
Compliant-opening prefilling is not tested. Suffix attacks are tested; target-model decoding is only compared in no-suffix baseline conditions, not as an attack intervention.
No weight or rank localization experiments.
No test of whether safety-training data or objectives cause shallow safety.
No training to deepen safety or evaluation of whether deepening holds up.

relationships.condition: Vicuna-7b, Vicuna-13b and Mistral-7b, which are chat-tuned. LIAR suffixes reach roughly 80-100% ASR@100 on AdvBench with 100 attempts.
relationships.reason: Suffixes defeat refusal on these models: r1 (97.12), r2 (79.81), r4 (96.15), r43-r44. The no-suffix baselines are far lower: r34, r35, r42. The same holds for the ablations r7-r12 and r15-r33, and for Vicuna-7b on MaliciousInstruct (r41).
relationships.display_finding: ASR@100 was 97.12, 79.81 and 96.15 on the three models, far above no-suffix baselines, and the ablations and Vicuna-7b on MaliciousInstruct showed the same pattern.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Vicuna-7b, Vicuna-13b and Mistral-7b, which are chat-tuned. LIAR suffixes reach roughly 80-100% ASR@100 on AdvBench with 100 attempts.
source_check.reason: Table 1 confirms r1/r2/r4 ASR@100 of 97.12/79.81/96.15. Table 10 confirms substantially lower no-suffix Vicuna baselines. Support concerns suffix attacks within the stated attempt budget.

relationships.condition: Llama2-7b chat target, and the Llama2/Llama3/Llama3.1 targets in Appendix E.1 Table 7
relationships.reason: LIAR gets only 3.85 ASR@100 on Llama2-7b (r3). Suffix attacks bypass safety on weakly defended models but not on the most robust one. Table 7 gives the other Llama results, which are not extracted as rows.
relationships.display_finding: LIAR reached only 3.85 ASR@100 on Llama2-7b chat. Suffix attacks bypassed weakly defended models but not this most robust one.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Llama2-7b chat target, and the Llama2/Llama3/Llama3.1 targets in Appendix E.1 Table 7
source_check.reason: Table 1 confirms r3 ASR@100 of 3.85. Table 7 reports low but nonzero success across these Llama targets; this supports model-dependent limitations, rather than absence of bypass. Its GPT2 Llama2 result is 5.77, distinct from Table 1.

relationships.condition: Reduced suffix diversity: low temperature, short suffixes
relationships.reason: ASR@100 falls to 84.62 at temperature 0.1 (r22) and 66-70 at temperatures 10 and 4 (r13, r14). It is 72.12 with 8-token suffixes (r23). Success depends on suffix diversity and on best-of-N sampling, though it stays substantial.
relationships.display_finding: ASR@100 fell to 84.62 at temperature 0.1, to 66–70 at temperatures 10 and 4, and to 72.12 with 8-token suffixes. Success depends on suffix diversity and best-of-N sampling, though it stays substantial.

source_check.notes: Section 5.4 says target responses use 30 tokens, while Table 6 and its discussion specify a 32-token default; both row descriptions follow explicit source statements. ASR uses refusal-keyword matching, with prompt drift and false positives acknowledged; repeated table entries and ablations are not independent evidence.

reader_labels.condition: Llama2-7b target; low-suffix success settings and no-suffix control conditions
reader_labels.reason: LIAR success is very low on Llama2-7b even at 100 attempts (r3); shorter suffixes and high-temperature suffix generation also have lower success (r13-r14, r23), and no-suffix controls are generally much lower than suffix attacks (r34-r36, r42).
